Nearly — sorted, yes, but a set drops the duplicate 1.

hints: Two facts: sets have no duplicates, and TreeSet iterates in sorted order.
exercises.solution: A `TreeSet` keeps one copy of each element in ascending order, so it prints **`[1, 4, 5]`**. A `HashSet` would also drop the duplicate, but its printing order would be unspecified; `LinkedHashSet` would give `[5, 1, 4]`, the order of first insertion.

hints: Follow one element at a time: 1 becomes 10 (rejected), 2 becomes 20 (rejected)...
As soon as an element passes the filter, `findFirst` has its answer.
exercises.solution: Elements flow through the pipeline one at a time. 1 → 10 (fails the filter), 2 → 20 (fails), 3 → 30 (passes), and `findFirst` stops the stream. `map` ran **3** times. (The one-element array is a common trick to have a lambda update a counter, since lambdas may only capture variables that are effectively final.)
`joining("-", "<", ">")` puts `-` between the elements, `<` before the first and `>` after the last: **`<x-y-z>`**.

exercises.prompt: A web crawler must remember which of several million URLs it has already visited, and check each new link against that memory. Order does not matter. Which is the best choice?

options.label: `HashSet<String>`
options.feedback: Yes. Membership tests take constant time on average, and duplicates are ignored automatically.

options.label: `ArrayList<String>` with `contains`
options.feedback: Not yet — `contains` on a list scans it, so each check costs time proportional to millions of entries.

options.label: `TreeSet<String>`
options.feedback: Not yet — it works, at O(log n) per check, but you would pay for sorted order you do not need.

options.label: `LinkedList<String>`
options.feedback: Not yet — the same linear scans as ArrayList, with more memory and worse cache behaviour.

hints: The key operation is "have I seen this before?". Which structure answers it fastest?
exercises.solution: **`HashSet<String>`**: `add` and `contains` are O(1) on average, so a million checks cost about a million steps. With a list, each check is O(n) and the total becomes quadratic, the classic performance bug. TreeSet is correct but slower, and only worth it if you need the URLs in order.

exercises.prompt: Which statements about `List.of(...)`, `Set.of(...)` and `Map.of(...)` are true? Choose all that apply.

options.label: They reject `null` elements, keys and values
options.feedback: Yes. Passing null throws a NullPointerException.

options.label: `Set.of` and `Map.of` iterate in the order you wrote the elements
options.feedback: Not yet — their iteration order is deliberately unspecified. Use LinkedHashSet or LinkedHashMap if you need insertion order.

options.label: If the elements are mutable objects, the objects inside can still change
options.feedback: Yes. Unmodifiable describes the collection, not its elements.

hints: Unmodifiable is a property of the container. What about the things it contains?
exercises.solution: **a**, **b** and **d**. The factory methods return unmodifiable collections that forbid nulls. Their iteration order (for sets and maps) is unspecified on purpose, so code cannot come to depend on it. And because only the container is unmodifiable, an immutable result also needs immutable elements, such as strings or records of immutable values.
